evidence.text: This one's really tough for me. I'm not sure if I'm looking at the next SurveyMonkey or MailChimp kind of opportunity that seems really straightforward, excellent execution and ends up being 50 or 100 times bigger at scale than it looks on the surface. Or if I'm looking at a business that's very good and very solid but has some kind of natural cap on scale. And it has all the elements that I like to see. I believe the network effects part of your audience recruitment piece. I believe the software piece. There's something about it, it's like a near fit. The pieces don't exactly fit together for me. And I can't, I've been struggling for the last 15 minutes to figure out what it is. And I don't think I'm going to get there. And I don't think it's anything you didn't say. I think this is one of the clearest, strongest presentations I've seen on The Pitch.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Awesome. So hey everyone. My name's Dennis. I'm one of the cofounders and I'm the CEO of User Interviews. Before I get started, any of you log into Myspace this morning?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Myspace?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: My rock and roll page.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I invested in Myspace at one point.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: I figure you probably didn't log in this morning. Anybody get here on a Segway?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: And then last one, anybody wearing Google Glass today?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: The common thread here, all three of these products are widely considered to be failures. And super expensive failures right? And the thing is, thousands of products fail every single year. My last startup was one of them.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's good.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: And the number one reason products fail, is that they don't understand their users and they build a product that their users don't want. Luckily there's a super easy solution here. You talk to your users. And so that's where we come in. We've built a software platform that makes it super easy for companies to bring in their users for any type of product or market research. And so that's why companies like Spotify, Pinterest, Wayfair and Vistaprint, and hundreds of others are using our platform every single month.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So we're raising $4 million. The goal here is to get our platform at every company so they can make better decisions and ultimately better products.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Can you give us an example of how that works?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So the first thing, we think of ourselves as the coordination layer, the participant management layer and the logistics layer. We are not the platform where people actually conduct the tests. So I'll explain more holistically how that works. I see your brow is furrowing. [laughter]

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So the first thing that happens is a product manager, a designer or a marketer basically decides they have some sort of question that they need to talk to users about. Our platform then goes to work and manages all the logistics behind screening candidates, gathering more information about them, figuring out who you want to invite, then inviting those users to the study, and then paying them for their time. So ultimately, we're the platform that makes sure that the person you want to talk to shows up at the right spot when you want to talk to them.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Sounds like you're just doing the logistics of it. You're arranging the meeting, you're having them come in.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You're providing them high quality...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Sending the reminders. And paying them.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: We provide the people, one. Or they can upload their own. And then we provide basically a workflow automation.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So how do you charge Wayfair? Walk us through the revenue.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah umm, we charge per participant that we recruit for one of our client studies.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And what's average of that?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: On average, it's $30 per participant.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It sounds like in a lot of ways what you're doing…

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Sorry, I do want to answer the last part of the question, because I think this is important. And so there's basically two parts of our product today. The first is the workflow that I walked you guys earlier, where you can come through, you can invite people from our audience or yours, we manage all the logistics. The second part of the platform is what we're calling our research hub. The research hub we just launched a couple months ago. That's a subscription offering. And that's for companies that want to be tracking their users across the entire company. And so they're paying a monthly fee for that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How much.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Ah so, we're in the middle of closing our first, it's about a $42,000 annual contract.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Who do you see as your most direct competitors?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: we see people using Google spreadsheets and Excel, and even Salesforce and HubSpot. The difference there is that they don't offer any of the workflow automations that we do, so they're not built for this research use case.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And how are you better, different, complementary?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah so what we're doing is we're taking that data that they fill out and we're using that to enhance the profiles of all the participants in our audience. And that makes us better at finding participants for the companies that we're working with moving forward. And if one company comes to us and asks a series of questions we capture that data they've asked, and then if another company comes and asks similar questions, we know who to target to deliver participant…

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: You're saying, you're building up profiles about the participants by the surveys they're completing.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Tell us a little bit about your experience. Your background.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. So I was a computer science major at Yale. Graduated in 2012. Worked in consulting for a year. That's where I met my first cofounder. We worked there for about a year. Had an itch to start building products. I talked about my first company that failed. It was a mobile app for business travelers. We built product for a year, year and a half, picked our heads up and had no users. umm That's when we started realizing, okay, let's talk to users, let's figure out how to solve this problem. Yeah, my wife said I shouldn't say this on air. But we basically... Our solution was to go buy refundable plane tickets, go sit at airport security, and then just talk to people waiting for their flights.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So in your, in your failed company, you're saying you couldn't find users? Or you couldn't find people to survey to get input?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So we... Both.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Both. Okay.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: But on the second front, we were trying to get people to give us feedback on the product.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And you couldn't get...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You didn't know where to find them?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: And we didn't know where to find them. We went to airports.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I think that's brilliant.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So this new company is solving a problem that you were experiencing with your old company?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I want to throw something out and see how you respond to this. What if I told you that I think there's a chance that you may be totally wrong.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I want to throw something out and see how you respond to this. What if I told you that I think there's a chance that you may be totally wrong. There's something that's been bothering me since you started.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I think that if you look at the trend of AI right now, the trend is that the part of artificial intelligence which is getting really cheap and really, really good, is prediction. Not judgment, but prediction. And I would hazard a guess that the company that'll do better than you, what it'll be a company that gets out there and goes up to Wayfair and saying “these three tables with these three colors are going to be the next things you should build. And it'll be much more reliable than you getting in humans into a room, getting everybody for 30 bucks and whatever. I think I could invest in your company, and I think for the next two, three years you can make some money. But I don't think you're going to be right for long, because I believe we have to wipe out all the people, and you have to make a prediction engine that does way better than what you're doing. Because prediction, as math gets cheap, prediction gets really, really, really useful.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. So here's why you're wrong. So ... There's two reasons. Before a product goes live, you need to figure out what to build. You need to figure out what direction you want to invest your resources in as a company. Before you actually have a product that you can test out there. And so that's why you need to have conversations with users to guide that before you actually have a tangible product that you want to predict something about. The second point about AI and predictions. So I just had a conversation two days ago with a director of user research at Microsoft. And the way he sees the world evolving is that there's a lot of tech around emotional analysis, basically you know face analysis of what people's emotions are as you're having a conversation. There definitely is going to be an overlap between AI and these conversations.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So how come Amazon, the entire Amazon runs on prediction engines.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Amazon has a massive user research team.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Right. And they're pulling people into rooms all the time at $30 a head?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So that's how they're scaling Amazon? Through rooms of users?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. So Microsoft, they're expecting to bring in 100,000 people over, maybe not next year but in a couple years down the line.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So the trend on Amazon and Microsoft is more people in rooms and less AI?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: I wouldn't say less. I think that they're complementary. You have to do both of them. And Amazon is releasing production code every eleven seconds. Umm they have to decide...

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So you believe in the future that rooms will get bigger, more people and prediction will just follow it?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I don't think AI is going to replace the touch...

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Hold on, I want to see him do it.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So we think they have to be complementary.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: And that's a big piece of it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: By the way, you're doing a very good job of controlling the flow of this pitch. Because we're all trying to pull you in different directions and I think you're just doing a really good job of keeping us...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: We're testing you.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: On task. And on schedule. And that doesn't always happen here.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah, I found that if I don't finish, people make assumptions if I don't answer questions. And it gets messy.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: No, that's really, really good.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What's the size of the addressable market, would you say?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. So ultimately, any company that builds a product, we think will be a user of what we're building. And so there are 3 million product companies out there, in industries that we're already working with. And so even if each of those spends $100 a month, that's a $4 billion opportunity.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: How do you price your enterprise product?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So to give you an example. There's a music streaming company that has hundreds of employees. So they have 50 full-time researchers, plus 300 plus employees full-time, like product managers, designers, marketers. So between them, they're spending $40 million on their product team that's trying to build better products. For us, we make them all more efficient. We think that's easily a $400,000 opportunity for us, and that's what we're going after. We've already started penetrating that organization.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay, so slow down. You've just told me that you believe your average ticket size is $400,000? Because that's my question. What do you think your average enterprise ticket price is?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. So it will be in the range of 50 to 60,000.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay. That sounds more right to me.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: But as we get to... So first thing that we'll do is we'll get every researcher at this company using the product. And that's the first 50,000.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Well, you think, right? So that's your supposition. So you think there's a land and expand program?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: And what are you telling your investors for by the end of 2019 your sales are going to be?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: We expect it to be about $5 million run rate.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: ARR run rate?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: And how much of that is your front end vs your back end?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So just to give you a context behind that $5 million. We've grown 10% month over month since we raised our seed round February of 2017. We went from $25,000 a month to $150,000 a month in bookings. And so even if we just continue that 10% month-over-month growth, that's what gets us to that 5 million run rate. You have another question. Just want to follow up on that. To the split between how much of that is going to be software, how much of that is going to be recruiting, we expect it to be about 30% software 2019, but then 50 - 60% software by end of 2020.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay. So let me rearticulate your business for you so I understand it. And please tell me if I'm wrong. You have very nascent revenue on the enterprise. Most of it is on the survey side and the front. And you're raising 4 million now.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay. And you think your average ticket price is going to be around $50,000 and you're going to land and expand. Which is by the way typical.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. But to, I think the one nuance here is that these companies that will be on this $50,000 ticket price, we're not going in cold and saying... We're already there. They're already spending 10, $20,000 a month with us. And so we're going to go in and say, look, all of your teams are already using our platform. Some of them for the recruiting. Some of them for the software piece.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: But you're still in a kind of a bit of a test track. I mean, no I admire the confidence. But the test track still is, for this company, would you agree with me, that for this company to be worth a lot of company, that software side needs to really, really grow?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: And the part that's worth more hasn't really started yet. And that's where you are.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yeah. I mean, if you want me to admit that on air, like yes.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I'm not trying... You're not on trial. What I'm trying to do is ask where you are because you're asking us for money. Because there's a big difference between saying, I think people are going to spend 400 grand or 50 grand, or whether you've done it not. That's like, that's a very big distance, right?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: No, understood. No. Totally understand. And I think there is partially a leap of faith in this round.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay, what was it the last round? Or how much have you raised?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: We raised a SAFE at an 8 million valuation.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: 8 million? Okay.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: And how much?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: So we've ultimately raised 1.7 million total.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay, now you're doing 4 million?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: At what valuation?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: That's for I think you guys to decide.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: What do you think the valuation is?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: I think fairly we would expect to be in the $18 million range.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: M-hm.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: A-ha.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: I mean I think, we're not trying to give away a third of the company on this round. I think based on the pipeline and once you see the companies that we're already in and how we expect to grow from what they're spending with us today to getting to those $50,000 contracts, we don't think that's a huge leap.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Let me just parrot back your number to you right. So at the end of 2019, about $2 million will be enterprise revenue, right?

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: The way you're defining enterprise, you're talking about the software piece?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Sure. Yes.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So if you put a 10x on that, where you're going to be in a year from now, it's worth about 20 million.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Well, so, you're discounting the other side of the business to zero, which I don't think is entirely fair.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Give it something. But I'm saying, okay 20, 25 million at best if you hit your numbers exactly. In a year from now.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: I think that's right. I think if you want to value the business strictly off of multiples, I think that is a way that you can look at it. Like honestly, we're not optimizing for price. We're optimizing for people that understand the vision, can add value to us as we grow to that next stage.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Well, no, that's not true. You just said, five minutes ago, you said I'm not going to give up a third of my company. So you are optimizing for price.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: A third of the company at 4 million would be 12 million dollars.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Right. So I'm just saying to you it is about price as well.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Yes. I think there's an absolute floor to the price. I think there's a floor to the price. We're definitely not going below 12 million.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: This one's really tough for me. I'm not sure if I'm looking at the next SurveyMonkey or MailChimp kind of opportunity that seems really straightforward, excellent execution and ends up being 50 or 100 times bigger at scale than it looks on the surface. Or if I'm looking at a business that's very good and very solid but has some kind of natural cap on scale. And it has all the elements that I like to see. I believe the network effects part of your audience recruitment piece. I believe the software piece. There's something about it, it's like a near fit. The pieces don't exactly fit together for me. And I can't, I've been struggling for the last 15 minutes to figure out what it is. And I don't think I'm going to get there. And I don't think it's anything you didn't say. I think this is one of the clearest, strongest presentations I've seen on The Pitch.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Agree.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It just for some reason I can't seem to get there on the absolute size of the opportunity. And I wish I could give you a clearer reason as to why.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: No. Appreciate that.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So I'll go. You might be surprised by me saying this, but actually I'm quite interested. I think you're super smart and I like the argument and I like the back and forth. And I enjoy the way you thoughtfully argue with us. I think you've got a lot going for you. I would like to come into your round. I think you're super smart. I like your hustle and my gut's good about this one.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Thank you. Appreciate it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How much are you going to invest?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I think I'd put, either between 50 to 150,000.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Great. Love to continue the conversation and keep that going.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I have sort of similar feelings. I have a really good feeling about you. You're obviously very bright. Early stage, but it seems that you're growing quickly. 10% month over month. And you're at good revenues so far. You're smart enough to realize that it would make a lot of sense to introduce a recurring revenue product, which you're doing. And for me, I obviously need to see what the valuation is to see what I'm investing in. But I'd like to invest 300,000.

turns.speaker: Dennis
turns.text: Very cool. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay. Okay. Um. So um... I love logistics. I love logistic companies. And interestingly enough I was just speaking at a CTO conference. umm And had a lot of the product designers there. And this is one of the conversations that kept coming up. And it is amazing how immersed they are in the users. More so than they said that they have ever been. They were saying, that they use every opportunity to talk about a product and try something out. And so this is just, umm this is a constant problem. But a very fascinating space. So I'd like to commit right now $100,000 of my own money as an angel.
